html:
The move of about six million African Americans from the rural South to cities in the North and West of the United States between about 1910 and 1970.

They left to escape Jim Crow segregation, lynching and the poverty of sharecropping. When World War I cut off immigration from Europe, factories in the North needed workers. Black newspapers such as the Chicago Defender urged people to come. A second, larger wave followed during and after World War II.

The main destinations were Chicago, Detroit, New York, Philadelphia, and later Los Angeles and Oakland.

The migration changed the country:

  • It made Black communities a political force in Northern cities.
  • It fed the Harlem Renaissance and carried jazz and the blues north.
  • Migrants still faced discrimination in jobs and housing, and white mobs attacked them, as in the riots of 1919.

The movement helped build support for the civil rights campaigns that won the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
sum: The move of about six million African Americans from the rural South to cities in the North and West of the United States between about 1910 and 1970.
